p: A real battery is an **ideal source of emf in series with an internal resistance r**.
When a current flows, **Ir volts are lost inside**, so the terminal pd is **emf − Ir**.
With no current, the terminal pd equals the emf.

rules: **S open (I = 0):** no lost volts, so the voltmeter reads the **emf**, 12 V.
**S closed:** lost volts = Ir = (2)(0,5) = 1 V, so the voltmeter reads 12 − 1 = **11,00 V**.
The **padlocks**: the emf and r belong to the battery and stay the same.

screens.q: Which sentence is the SAGS definition of emf?
choices: The emf is the voltage of the battery.
Not the SAGS sentence: it does not say energy per coulomb.
The emf is the total energy supplied per coulomb of charge by the cell.
The SAGS sentence, used in the 2018, 2021 and 2023 November memos.
The emf is the energy per electron.
The emf is per coulomb of charge, not per electron.

screens.q: A lamp is switched on, and the voltmeter across the battery now reads less than before.
choices: Pieter: The emf has dropped, because the lamp uses some of it.
The emf belongs to the battery and stays the same.
Lerato: The emf has not changed. A current now flows, so there are lost volts (Ir) inside the battery, and the terminal pd is less.
Only I, Ir and the terminal pd changed.
Thabo: The internal resistance has gone up, because current now flows through it.
r belongs to the battery and stays the same.
screens.why: Lerato ✓. The emf and r belong to the battery and stay the same ✓; only I, Ir and the terminal pd changed ✓.

p: **emf = V_{load} + V_{internal resistance} = I(R_{ext} + r)** (data sheet). V_{internal resistance} = Ir, the lost volts. The memo form is V_{load} = emf − Ir.
① No current? A voltmeter across the battery reads the emf.
② Current flowing? Lost volts = Ir, and V_{load} = emf − Ir.
③ To find r: r = (emf − V_{load}) ÷ I.

screens.h: Worked example 11.3: two readings of one voltmeter
screens.q: “In the circuit below, a battery with internal resistance is connected to a circuit with a 20 Ω resistor, an ammeter and a switch.” “When the switch is open, the voltmeter reads 12 V and when it is closed, it reads 10 V.” (a) Define emf. (2) (b) “Write down the emf of the battery.” (1) (c) “Calculate the internal resistance of the battery.” (5)

lines.x: The emf is the total energy supplied ✓ per coulomb of charge by the cell ✓.

lines.side: no current, so no lost volts

traps: 10 V is the terminal pd while a current flows. With the switch open there are no lost volts.

ask.prompt: Work out the current with the switch closed.

traps: With the switch closed the 20 Ω has the terminal pd, 10 V, not 12 V.
The lost volts are 2 V, and r = 2 ÷ 0,5.
The 20 Ω is outside the battery. r = lost volts ÷ I.

why: With S closed, why is the 10 V the pd across the 20 Ω?
The voltmeter across the battery reads the terminal pd ✓, and the 20 Ω is the only external resistor ✓. The lost volts are 12 − 10 = 2 V = Ir.

screens.q: A battery of emf 12 V delivers a current of 2 A, and the voltmeter across its terminals reads 10 V. Calculate the internal resistance.

traps: That is 10 ÷ 2, the external resistance. r = lost volts ÷ I.
num.hint: Lost volts = 12 − 10 = 2 V. r = lost volts ÷ I.

screens.why: V_{load} = emf − Ir: 10 = 12 − 2r, so r = 1,00 Ω.

screens.q: A voltmeter across a battery reads 9,0 V with the switch open, and 8,1 V when a current of 0,6 A flows. Calculate r.

traps: That is the lost volts. Now divide by the current.
That is 9,0 ÷ 0,6. Use the lost volts: 9,0 − 8,1.
num.hint: The emf is 9,0 V. Lost volts = 9,0 − 8,1. r = lost volts ÷ I.

screens.why: emf = 9,0 V; lost volts = 0,9 V; r = 0,9/0,6 = 1,50 Ω.
